reading.rtitle: What the Interview Is Really For
paras: For nine years I interviewed applicants for the college I graduated from. I met them in coffee shops, in public libraries and, more recently, through a laptop screen, and I wrote a short report after every conversation. Over those years I came to believe that most applicants misunderstand what the interview is for, and that the misunderstanding costs them more than nerves ever do.

The first misunderstanding is that the interview is a test. It is not. I did not have the applicant's grades, and I was explicitly asked not to request them. There were no correct answers to memorize and no questions designed to trap anyone. The interview is better described as an evaluative conversation: evaluative, because I did write a report; conversation, because the report was almost entirely about whether a real exchange of ideas had taken place.

The second misunderstanding follows from the first. Believing they are about to be tested, many students prepare by rehearsing answers, and rehearsed answers are surprisingly easy to recognize. They arrive too quickly, they are slightly too complete, and they rarely respond to the exact question that was asked. A student who has memorized ninety seconds on leadership will deliver those ninety seconds whether I ask about leadership, failure or a favorite book. The result sounds polished and feels empty, and I would often find myself unable to remember a single detail by the time I sat down to write.

What I did remember were anecdotes. A student who told me about repairing a neighbor's bicycle, and then explained what she had learned about patience, gave me a far better sense of who she was than any list of achievements. I also remembered pauses. When a student said that was a hard question and asked for a moment to think, the answer that followed was almost always more interesting than the answers that came instantly. Composure, I learned, is not the absence of hesitation. It is the ability to hesitate without panic.

Spoken answers also have a shape that written ones do not. On the page, a dense sentence full of nominalizations can be admirable; across a table, the same sentence forces the listener to hold too much in memory at once. The students I remember best seemed to understand this instinctively. They offered a short answer first, then a story, then a sentence explaining what the story meant, and they signaled each move with a small phrase, such as the short answer is, or what I mean by that is. I could follow them without effort, and so I could pay attention to what they were actually saying rather than to how they were saying it.

It is also worth saying what interviewers are not looking for. We are not looking for the most articulate student in the room, and we are certainly not looking for someone who has read every book we mention. Several of my strongest reports described students who were visibly nervous, who admitted what they did not know, and who asked me a genuine question about my own experience. Rapport is not charm. It is curiosity that goes in both directions.

My advice is therefore modest. Prepare to talk about the things you actually care about, not to recite them. Know two or three stories well enough to tell them differently each time. And when you do not know what to say, say so, take a breath and think. That short, honest pause may be the moment your interviewer remembers best.

gist.prompt: Which statement best captures the writer's main point?
choices: The interview is the most important part of a college application and must be carefully rehearsed.
The interview is an evaluative conversation, and genuine stories, pauses and curiosity matter more than polished answers.
Interviewers mainly want applicants who are confident, charming and never hesitate.

items.situation: Say it with structure: an interviewer asks, "Why art history?"
tips: The short answer is that I want to understand the decisions behind what we see.
Short answer first; offer the longer one.

items.situation: Reformulate: you just said "I like looking at art" and it sounded vague.
tips: What I mean by that is that I notice how small choices change what a painting does.

items.situation: Qualify softly: you love famous museums, but your key moment was elsewhere.
tips: I love the big museums. That said, the moment that mattered was in a tiny gallery.
That said: a qualification without a fight.

items.situation: Buy time honestly: "What is something you have changed your mind about?"
tips: That is a good question. Let me think for a second.
Name the pause, then take it. No fillers.

items.situation: Return and close: you digressed about a museum guard for thirty seconds.
tips: So, to come back to your question, that is why I care about how we look.
Show that you never lost the thread.

items.situation: Ask your own question at the end of the interview.
tips: What is something about the college that surprised you when you arrived?
A genuine question builds rapport in both directions.

listenings.text: Good evening, everyone. I run the interview program, so let me explain what actually happens after you apply. Most of our interviews are conducted by volunteer graduates of the college, people who live in or near your region and who give up an evening because they remember what it felt like to be seventeen. These days many of the conversations happen online. Now, the question I get most often is how much the interview counts. The honest answer is that it is one piece among many. It very rarely decides an application on its own. What it can do is add real color to a file, a sense of the person behind the grades and the essays. I read hundreds of interview reports every year, and I can tell you what the strongest ones say. They almost never say the applicant was impressive. They say something like, I would happily have kept talking for another hour. And very often they add that the student asked the interviewer a genuine question, and actually listened to the answer.

So my interview was in a coffee shop, and it was going fine until the interviewer asked, what book changed your mind about something? And I froze. My brain just started listing famous books I thought would sound impressive, and I actually began to talk about one I had only half read. About twenty seconds in, I could see in her face that she knew. So I stopped. I said, sorry, that is a really good question, can I have a second to think? And she said, of course. And then I told her the truth, which was that the book that changed my mind was a comic book about a family of immigrants, and it made me stop being embarrassed about my grandparents' accent. We talked about that for fifteen minutes. I found out later that she was the daughter of immigrants herself. What I learned is that a pause you actually name sounds much more confident than a rehearsed answer, and that telling the truth is what turned the interview into a conversation.
